blocks.x: Okay. Tim can look at it and see if it's working. If you want to turn it around towards you. Yeah, let's see. Let's all say our names. It's the first reel, so we want to get that down on there. Okay.
Well, I'm Don Albert.
Yeah, and Tim? Tim Gibson. How's your voice picking up? Is it picking up okay?
It seems to be okay.

Okay, and I'm Dick Allen. Alright. So, I've got a ton of questions to ask you. Okay, Dick. Sounds great. Since Tim is here, I thought maybe we could get into the business of, you know, what it's like running a band. Like, how about, did you have a music librarian? How did you keep all the parts straight in other words?

Well, each musician had his own book. However, at the end of the, the conclusion of the performance at night, we would put them all in one big trunk that we had. And we had the guys that would drive the bus and you, well, the regular maintenance man, we call them, and valets, and they would take care of all the music, put it in one great big trunk.
How many people travel with the band, other than the musicians?
Well, we, I have had as high as 21, including wives and new members of the band, some prospects that wanted to join the band, sometimes as high as 21.
Well, you would have a, you'd have a valet?

We had two. We had a fellow that drove the bus, Wilbur Usand, and another, one named Luther, from Little Rock, that did all of the setting up and taking down to the band, and driving the bus, and different things like that.
Well, would they be responsible if something got misplaced?
Well, in a way, in a way they'd be responsible if we could tie it down and it was stolen or something through negligence, but that never happened.
No, but I mean, you know, you, I don't know about your uniforms or the pieces of music if something got out of place.

Well, that very seldom happened, but that was the responsibility of the individual himself to take care of his, his clothing and his music and different things like that. In those days, it was, most everybody had to be on their own. It's not like it is today where there's a man, almost a ballet for each musician. In those days, it was just one of these things where you had to take care of your own business.
Well, get rid of my coat while we're talking about valets and all that.
Right, but you don't have a valet right now. No, I'll be comfortable.
Anyway, the way I would see it, you'd want to get to the job and you'd allow some time to get dressed and stuff. I mean, you'd might be a man.

Well, most of the times we always got in town early in the morning and gave us time to find a place to rest and clean up and get ready about 8, 8, 8.30 at night and go right to the dance halls. And when we finished that night, if the next jump was 150, 200, 300 miles, we'd leave right after the dance so we could make the next town.
But did you have any dressing rooms in these dance halls?
No, very seldom, very seldom. We possibly would dress at the places where we were staying, private homes. Or if the dance hall was big enough with facilities in it, we would use it.
Did you have any uniforms?

I think my band was one of the best dressed bands on the road in those days. We had three or four sets of uniforms. And what were they? Well, some of the pictures you have seen, I know that you've seen different types of uniforms. Mostly a suit.
Well, that's right. You told me you were in touch with tailors. We talked about tailors in one fall. That's right. That's right. You knew them. They were special tailor-made?

That's right. The first one we had made was one of the finest tailors in the state of Texas, possibly in the United States. His name was Goldberg. And those suits we had then today would sell about three, four, five hundred dollars. I think we got them for about sixty bucks, which in those days was a tremendous price.
And your tires and shirts, did they match?
Well, yes. Everyone tried to have the same thing, even including the shoes.
How about lights in the dance hall? Did y'all have lights?

Just ordinary lights. Wasn't anything fantastic like it is today. Just regular lighted place, electric lights. That's all. Not any fantastic lighting like it is today. What about the theaters? The theaters were all right. We played the theaters up in the upper state New York Palace Theater there. And we played a couple of theaters in New York City. And we played over other parts of the country, like the Earl and the Fox. Well, the lighting there was all right. It's not like it is today, but it was fantastic. And it had spotlights. Yes, it was fantastic for those days.
Yeah, so I see. All right. But you set up music stands, I guess.
That is right. We had the music stands with the Don Albin on the front.
And you said Don Albin on the front.

And of course it carried the little small electrical attachments that would be not visible to the audience, but it would shine down on the music, which made the thing look like it was in darkness. But to us the lights were on the stand. But most of the times, these guys had memorized all of these arrangements. They just put it up there for a guideline. But they knew the book to memory. Unless it was one or two, maybe three or four new arrangements came in. And then they would have to learn those. But sooner or later they got rid of those and just went straight with the book.
When you were working on the percentage, you would watch the game.

Well, now there you go again. A lot of times they asked me why did I stop playing like I did. Well, for more reasons than one. That was one of them to stay on the door and watch the proceedings there and make sure that I got everything was mine. That's what happened when we were on the verge of being lynched in Thomasville, Georgia, playing a percentage dance and the school teacher had charge of the dance. And naturally I was up there checking the door with him when the policemen came in to arrest everybody, including the band and me. I took the money out of the drawer and put it in my pocket to make sure that I wasn't going to be on the losing end all the way around. But I was on the losing end because in a way when this fellow, the captain, whoever he was, arrested the whole band and arrested me and attempted to shoot me six of them in the hall. Well, they got us down to the jailhouse and I had given one of the girls in the band that used to dance. Her name was James. Her last name was James. And I had given her most of the money to hold so when we got into the jailhouse, it was a small place. They put 19 of us in one room. But a couple of the guys had gotten away and Mickey Alcorn happened to be one of them. And Kato was the bass player. And they had torn up all the instruments. The guys had just thrown chairs and everything else. They're the ones that started to fight. So this officer there, I guess he was a captain, he told me to put my money out of my pocket on the table. So I put what I had in my pocket, which a monitor made about $35 or $40. And he told me, well, that wasn't enough. I want all the money. And he said, you're over there charging those. Well, can I use the words that he used? He says, you're charging those niggers too much money over there, 75 cents a head to hear that rock music. And he said, that's too much money. And he said, I know you got more money than that. Well, I said, yes, possibly so. I said, but all I have is what I've put there. He said, well, I want all of the money. So I told the girl to put the money on the desk and she counted it out to him. Well, I said, I'd like to have a receipt for that money. He said, this is going to be a fine. And he called me a smart nigger from New York and of course, showed you how stupid he was. The license on the bus was Texas license. Well, to make a long story short, I asked him for a trial before a judge. And he said, well, I'm setting this fine where this judge is going to set it. I'm sure he's going to set it like that. And there's an entrance and an outlet to Thomasville, Georgia. I want you to use both of them. See if you've already used the entrance and I use the exit. I told him, thank you. And got in the bus. Well, my father, I was traveling with him. He was acting as a bus driver in a valley. And we stopped in a service station on the way out. We're going to Macon, Georgia for the next night. Well, we were busted. We didn't have anything. So I asked the attendant there, would he trust me with 150 gallons of gas? Because that's what the bus used. It used 75 gallons on one side, one tank and 75 on the other tank. And I said, I would like to have five gallons of gas. Oh, you say, I mean, all right. He said, oh, you the fellas were in that trouble tonight. I said, that's right. I said, but if you trust me with this, as soon as I get to Macon, mister, I'll send you your money. He said, okay. And he filled up both of the tanks and gave me five gallons of gas. Well, as soon as I got to Macon, Georgia, I went to a doctor friend of mine and was connected with the promotion of the band, Dr. Frasier. And I told him the situation, how it was, and how bad it had been. He says, well, sure, we'll send a fella the money. So we sent it to him right away. And naturally from an incident such as that in the days, then the Pittsburgh Courier took up the complaint from me and they wrote a massive story on it. And that's one of the incidents that I have always wanted to talk to you about. I don't think I have ever talked to you on this thing before. That was one of the sad parts of being a Negro band and traveling through the south and things like that after they find out that you are a Negro band.

We have talked about it some, but I didn't get everything down, you know. Oh, we didn't? Yeah. Like that, you know, and every time you tell something you get more. Did you ever know a fella named Floyd Snellson?

Sure, Floyd was my publicity man. He was a great, great newspaper man, but he had a problem. Alcohol. But he was one of the greatest writers that you ever want to see. And on one of my band pictures you see Floyd Snellson leaning out of the window.

Yes. That's why I thought they didn't ask you about him because of Mickey. Right. How about him? Right. Why did you call him Mickey? Just a nickname. No, no, no, no. Mickey? No, no real reason for. For calling Mickey?
Yeah.
Well, I don't know. It had nothing to do with Mickey Mouse.
No, no, no. I don't guess because Mickey Mouse wasn't in order then.
Who just called him Mickey? Just came out.

Right. Yeah. Now, maybe he might remember why, but I don't know, but I remember this. Everyone, like I was talking to someone last night, oh, Cottrell was here last night, and Miss Simmons, my school teacher, was asking me why I continued to call him Bucks. Well, I said I called him Bucks, and I called him Riney, I said everybody in the band had nicknames. Even me, I was called the old man. I was 21 years old, but I was called the old man.
But, what was the Bucks having to do with it?
Bucks, just fatty old buckles. Oh, yeah. And we cut it off to Bucks. Oh, I see. And Riney? Riney, because, I don't know, because of his color.
Oh, I see. And Floyd Snelson was with you all the time?
No, no.
Did he handle several bands?
No, no, he didn't handle any bands. The Pittsburgh Courier had dropped him as a writer, and I picked him up. Oh, I see.
So, he only was with you.

Right. And he, yeah. But, of course, he also would write stories that the Pittsburgh Courier would take on his travels, not only for me, but for other things that he would encounter, which kept him getting a little few bucks here and there. But, he drank it as fast as he got his checks.
But, he must have been a pretty good writer. Beautiful. He got publicity.
And one of the greatest.
What about newspapers? Is there any other newspapers that you were in touch with, especially where Mike Luxembourg?

The Pittsburgh Courier was the biggest thing then, the Chicago Defender. I think most of those papers, the Pittsburgh Courier is still going, but I think the Chicago Defender has been deleted years ago.
Yeah, but there's a guy named Walter Allen is going through all, you know, the Baltimore for America.

Yeah. Well, most of the Negro papers had carried big stories. However, every white newspaper carried the stories when they came to town. Unfortunately, I didn't keep all of these write-ups, you know. You do have some scrapbooks, though, is it?

Oh, yes, I have worlds of scrapbooks. Do you want to get the picture to you? I think she got it. Okay. All right. Let's see. Well, back to business of just how you would get set up and everything. Did you ever have to rent pianos in those days?

No, usually the dance halls had them in there, but I had a very, very peculiar pianist. To me, he's one of the greatest, and you know who I'm referring to, Lloyd Glenn. And he was very picky about his pianos. And a lot of times we'd come to these dance halls, and the pianos were so low that we would have to tune up with the piano and change our whole way of playing. Because we couldn't reach the piano, or narrow to tune it. So if we tune with the piano, Lloyd Glenn would have to transpose maybe a tone or two above where we were playing. He didn't want that. And he just wouldn't play, so we'd play without a piano. Do you want him on the phone?
I don't know.
That was wonderful, not on the other phone. Oh, I see. I didn't answer upstairs. Yeah, well, we can turn it off for a second.
Sorry, man, I like this. It's skim milk. Oh, well, that's good for me.
Keep your weight down?
Oh, yeah.
It seems as though my brother-in-law has to be on the diet and he has to have skim milk.
Oh, thank you, Mr. Hollins. We were talking about the pianos and how he didn't want to... Right. ...dine's pose.
He wouldn't play on it, Dick. He was picky.
Yeah. And so you couldn't retune him, you just were there.
Oh, the band would just go ahead with us. Yeah, I know that.
What about... Oh, you would get your chords from another instrument, maybe?
Well, from the guitar or the banjo.
Did they have amplifiers there? No amplifiers. Did you ever use an amplifier? Yeah.

Only time, not that I can remember in the early days, we used a megaphone like we used to use for the singer. And all of this high-powered mechanism they have now, no, we didn't have anything like that. So that came in later? Later, yes. After your band broke up? Well, possibly maybe just before we used the old crystal mics. One stand, one crystal mic. Mostly for the singer. Oh. Yeah.

What about the... When you were in a theater, would there have any sort of special sets in those days? The drops, you mean the props? Yeah, the drops and all that. Not necessarily. Not for a band? No, not for a band. No, not for a band. How would you carry the instruments and the trunk with the music? Where would they be carrying in the bus?

Oh, we had a top on the bus and we also had the, on the inside, we had racks on the inside. But we used the top part for the trunks, the clothing and the inside for the instruments. And we were talking about that, how dangerous it could be. Yes, it was. In those days you didn't realize that. Good break there. Why sure. Good break things. Very easy.
What happened when somebody missed a rehearsal, by the way?
Didn't anybody miss any rehearsals.
You didn't never find them or anything? They just never missed?

They were more interested in rehearsing than they were doing in anything else, especially when they would get a new arrangement. There was no problem in the call rehearsal. They'd be up all night and get up and rehearse again.
You were speaking about all your individuals carrying their own music. Right. How many arrangements would you carry at one time? The whole book. How many would that be?
About 150, 200. The books were about 20 inches thick.
They all fit in one folder?

One folder for each man and they would be put in the trunk in sequence. Alphabetical or numbered? Well, yes. The brass here, the reeds here, the rhythm here. The rhythm didn't necessarily carry any books.
How did you keep track of 150 arrangements at one time?
Well, they were numbered, one or nine. You play them so often it's just like running the ABCs.
You knew the numbers by head.
Right. Most of them. Well, I'll say 90% of them.
How did you program?

Well, there was no program. You're playing every night so you're almost following the same format. Unless there was a request within the area of time that you were playing and you would try to play the request, which would deviate just a little bit from the normal procedure every night.
You never had any printed program, anything you wrote up yourself and the numbers on?
No. No. That wasn't anything like that in those days.
Yeah, you did. I mean, it seemed to me yesterday at the concert that you had everything planned and you knew when we were talking about.

I did. I did. Because this is a different incident altogether. What we're talking about. We're talking about playing dances in the olden days. Well, you had a set format because you went to a different city every night. And possibly sometime you'd stop in a city maybe for two weeks and that was considered a big contract. And two weeks, man, we really had a rest. But yesterday, you're referring to yesterday at the concert, the reason why I had a list made is because of the new master ceremonies that was there. What was his name? Mel Levin? Mel Levin. In the past, Plato Smith has been the master ceremonies. I was just trying to familiarize him with the program. I didn't know you hadn't noticed that.

Well, I'm trying to notice everything, you know. Well, that's great. You're inquisitive. You told me about how nothing was rehearsed yesterday. That amazed me because the band, you know, everything was so pretty. All the hominis seemed right to me, you know.

Right. Well, we rehearsed but not at the place. We rehearsed over the telephone. Oh. How did I do that? Yeah. Okay. I discussed it with Freddie Coleman. I told him, I said, you know what I want you to do, don't you? What? I said, well, I want you to do the same thing that you did last year. Bring that tambourine and watch my tempos. Well, I tell you to cut him and cut out and just listen to me. And he laughed. He says, okay. So, I did the same thing with Walter Lewis, but Walter had just recently played a concert with me in San Antonio and he was familiar with most of the numbers. I just had to set him in the spots where I wasn't going to play him. And the same way with Cottrell. And plus, he, well, he's just a good man.
So, you had no problem. It's just the guys worked together. Right. And they knew that I could play three-part harmony if you wanted them.

Right. Well, you noticed the three-part harmony on Mood Indigo, the three-part harmony on Look Down at Lawson Road, which was the only ones that required a three-part harmony. The others was go as you see or as you feel.
And you used the tambourine just on one moment?

Well, the tambourine, yes. Because the tambourine was fitting into the story of jazz where it began with the slaves. And the slaves played the tambourines. That was one of the only instruments they could play. And finally, from there to maybe the guitar and then modulated on to the way it is now. And the tambourine was to give it the sort of a holy roller effect, as we call it. The way the slaves used to go from one thing to the other. That's why I was trying to tell Mel, you know, as much as I could, so he would go ahead and use his own words.
Tim came up with something about arrangements. Did you pay the men to do arrangements?

We didn't have any money to pay ourselves nothing. Would you have a bond for everybody in the band? Well, everybody in the band worked as a family. That's what it was. If we made ten dollars, we'd split ten dollars. By the same token, if we made a hundred, we'd split a hundred. And everybody wanted the band to be the best and everybody would chip in the things that they knew how. I think Cottrell made one or two arrangements. Herbert Hall made some. And of course we had Harold Holmes, who did a tremendous job of arranging. He was one of the bass players. But the first arranger I had in the band was Phil Tiller from Little Rock, Arkansas. That was the first arranger in 1929.
Who were the main arrangers?

There wasn't any main arrangers. Harold Holmes wrote his. Billy Douglas wrote his. And Herbert Hall. If a guy would get an idea, he would write it down. But no one was, you're referring to something like in Jimmy Luster's band, where Si Oliver was the main arranger.
Well, no, there might be five main arrangers and maybe one guy would only do two.

Well, and then you might have the thing that existed in Duke's band. Someone would write the score and Tizal would abstract it. We didn't have anything like this. The guy would write the arrangement. He would write his score and he would write each individual part for each musician.
So you didn't have any copies or anything like that? No copies. The guy would do the whole work from top to bottom. That's right. That must have had some morale in the band. Beautiful. Beautiful.

They really can. That's the thing. They got along. Beautiful as far as I can see. I never ran into a conflict where one guy would balk at doing this. Like I see today. There's no harmony there. But strange as it seems, everyone there got along real swell.
What about if a guy got sick? And you're on the road.

That's another question. It's hard for me to answer. I don't remember anybody getting sick, but one time was Turner, wasn't it? What about that? Well, that was in later years. But Henry Turner got real sick in a little town of Ashland, Kentucky, I think. It was in the hills. And we had to...no, I'm sorry. Another fellow, Buddy Collins. He was from here. I don't know if you ever hear any talk about him. He was a vocalist. You've told me about him. Yeah. Well, Nick Turner got sick in this little small town in the area. The undertaker wanted to bury him before he died. And we had to leave town. When we came back, we had to take Nick away from there. Because they were getting rid of him faster than where he was supposed to go. But he got over it. We often laugh about that. If we hadn't stayed away a couple of days, old Nick Turner would have been buried over there in Ashland.
I don't know if he's still going or not. You were going to say something?

Well, we've already passed it, but I didn't want to say nothing since you've heard of it. But you said about it being dangerous about the instruments. We played Austin one night, and they didn't steal the instruments there, but they stole seven trunks.
All the clothing. All the uniforms and their regular dress wear.
And that time in Greenland, where they broke your own instruments and the drums and all that?
No, no. I told Nick about that. That's in... Thomasville. Thomasville, Georgia.
Yeah, we were talking about that.
That was a put-up deal.
Yeah. All planned in the front. Right. Well, what about somebody like Jimmy Johnson? He couldn't have been young. The bass player? The bass player.
No, Jimmy was an old man.
But was he in shape enough to travel?

Sure he was. He was in beautiful health. He was a strong old man. And he still drank his whiskey, but he never was drunk on the job that I can remember. But Jimmy was strong, as strong as anyone in the band had to be to play the way he played. See, my band is one of the first bands to use a string bass. And I finally got two string basses in the band. Jimmy Johnson and Harold Holmes. Well, Harold was a different type of bass player. He was more modern than Jimmy, but Jimmy was more of a true bass player than he was. What do you mean? When I say true, I mean his notes were more perfect. And Harold would make a lot of notes, while Jimmy made just a few notes. But they sounded different and fill in a little bit more. And then, too, Harold was writing a lot of arrangements.
Well, Jimmy Johnson must have had a good ear then.
He did. He was mostly an ear player from the old days. But finally Jimmy did learn how to read bass parts enough to read bass parts.
Did you ever see him on a bicycle? Somebody was telling me he used to even ride a bicycle.

Well, if it was, it was in the days that he was playing here with Bunk Jones, not with Bunk, with what's the trumpet player, the first one? Buddy Bowling. Buddy Bowling. Maybe in those days he might have been a younger man. He might have rode a bicycle then. You mean with that bass on his back? Yeah. Yes, I've heard him say that. I mentioned Larry Cottrell's daddy yesterday at the concert. I used to lug those drums all the way from his house up to Clay Hall Street. And then there was a whole set of drums on his back.
Well, he had special drums, too, though, they said.
Well, not necessarily so. I never seen anything special about the drums. He had the same drums all the time. Oh, yeah. In those times.
Sure. They were just a regular set of drums.
Regular set of drums. Not collapsible or like that. Oh, no. Nothing in those days like that. But all in all, the concert yesterday was the best this year. What do you think about it?

Well, I want to ask you about some of the things. Because, well, you know, I had a marvelous time and everybody, as far as I was concerned, and the audience was having a marvelous time. Everybody, you know, I was watching all the people. And there's something that reminded me of something. What about the waltz medley? That's the first time I've ever seen anybody do a waltz medley at a concert. First, the waltz you say for me, and then let me call you sweet.

Well, did you understand the story behind it? I did. When I mentioned it. In the old days, the bands would play a waltz, and just as soon as the waltz was over, they'd go into the swing temple like that. That was the reason for playing it.

What about people in the audience of dancers? Would they ever sing or not? Yes, that was the tradition. And you got the people to do it yesterday. That was amazing. I never saw anybody do that at the jazz club. Well, I was. And you already had the audience in the party.

If you notice, I was trying, when I first announced my program, that I was going to play old numbers and new numbers. And I was going to give them an idea of what happened in the old days because being 65 years old yesterday, I could go back that far.
That sing along is good for the people. They like that, that they give out, look like, you know, and they do it at night.

You make them part of your program. Yeah. See, you make them part of it. Make them feel as though they're part of your program, and you're not just the thing up there doing your thing. They come there and enjoy themselves. So, it's just a night that I have of trying to study my audience and get them in with me, not me with them, see.

Well, I have noticed, I guess the tape's about to run out and I want to get in the middle of it, but we'll just have to stop. But I've noticed some showmanship and some of the big bands and some of the singers, they'll pull like an act right in the middle of something to create some sort of excitement. I see people faint, you know, they'll call the doctor in.
What's that to attract attention?
To attract attention to Chris.
Well, fortunately I never had to do anything like that.
You never did have to do any tricks at all. No, no, no fix. Yeah, but I, well, that's the end of the reel.
You did a little comedy. . . .
Yeah, we got it now. I just stepped on the microphone. Oh, that's great. It's still picking up though. Don't worry about it. You were talking about he used to do a comedy?

No, we did sort of a little show. During the course of the dance, we would say we're time now for a little floor show. We had the James sisters and Mickey and I would do a little scene. He would sit on my lap and I would finger his arm. Just something that deviated from the regular routine of playing numbers after number after number.
What was the Let Me Call You Sweetheart thing here? Why for example?

Well, she was discussing how I would announce that whether you're standing, sitting or dancing, whether you're here with your sweetheart or somebody else's wife, we're all going to get together and say Let Me Call You Sweetheart. There's one little bit he said we'll catch on with the audience.
And he'd say look into their eyes and sing that song to make a feel. Do you want to come closer? Should we pick up a picture?
It looks like it. I'm not sure.
Sure.
Sometimes they were in it with the sweetheart. Sometimes they were in it.

That's right. Sometimes they were with somebody else. He said, I remember who you're with. Turn around through him and look in her face and call him Sweetheart. See, they don't like it. Okay. But they do it too. At the keyhole. That was at the keyhole. Jack Willis.
Telephone. No, it's not Jack Willis.

I'll tell you when Jack came in. Jack didn't work in my band. Mm-hmm. But Jack did come to San Antonio when I'd given up the band with Freddie Coleman's little band at the first keyhole nightclub that I had. Mm-hmm. But there was a fellow yesterday at the concert that they very seldom mentioned around here. I thought was a great trumpet player. He played in my band. Joe Phillips. Yes.
Did you see Joe? I did. And he...
Now, he's another guy that did some arranging.

Yes. We talked about that. I talked to him on the phone, but he didn't recognize me on the phone. Excuse me. So he said he could tell me a lot more about it. You know when you call people up sometimes and they don't know you.

Well, people have a tendency today to ignore everybody. And fortunately, I'm not one of those. I love to talk and I love to find out who the person is that I'm talking to. Oh. But Joe Phillips never was a talker.

Mm-hmm. Oh. We were listening to the record this morning again. Which one? The one with your own band from 36. What one? Which one? The whole. Oh, the whole album? All eight sides. Right, right. How did you feel at the end of the day?
After recording? Mm-hmm. Fortunately, this was cut in less than three hours.

How many takes did you have to do? One. Just a one-take shot? One takes, but that's all. And what about with the blues singers and with Troy Floyd? That was in 26 and 27. Yeah, how many takes did you have to do that? One.

It was almost a full session, but what happened, you would rehearse the number first and when you thought you had it, but then you were ready to go into the mic. One mic. And it was spelled on that record, this little black thing would come off and they'd pull it up and pull it up. Like a thread. Like a thread. One take.
You say forced issue, you mean that's all they encouraged you to take?
That's right. That's right. Forced issue. A little different.
Yeah.

Well sure it is. A lot different. For instance, when I recorded for Salt Man, I know one time we played, and we were going to take it. And by the same token, we made one cut on one of the sides with the hammer, I think it was. I can't recall the name of the song, but we hit that and offered one take. But the rest of them, two, three, like that.
What about in the 1936 session with your own band? How would it pick up the band? Do you think it picked up the drums fully?
Well, you've heard the album.
Yeah, but I've never heard Fats Martin in person. Do you think it's fair to Fats Martin or fair to the rest of the band? Is it true to the band's sound is what I'm getting at?
I think it is. Yeah. But however, it could be, it would make a lot better today.
Yeah, it would be high fidelity today.

Why sure, why sure. You could cut each section out. Why is on this particular record, you have to let it play like it is. You can't show the reeds, you can't show the brass, you can't show the drums as you're referring to individually, which you can do today.
And what about in the Troy Floyd days?
Same thing.
It really didn't, it wasn't high fidelity, but it would pick up pretty much the sound.
Same thing because this is only, you're only talking about a year or two difference. Mm-hmm.
I've got so many things I want to ask you about and I hate to skip about, but tell me about booking syndicates in Texas and Oklahoma and Arizona and different places like that.
Yeah, you would deal with individuals, wasn't any big agencies.
Yeah, you would deal with one man?

One man. How much territory? The man that first picked me up was Bernard Galway. And I had him, not only was his name, but Rabinowitz. And then finally this Al Travis that was the biggest crook in the world. And then the next biggest crook was this one that I picked up here, Chauncey Highland, on the revision of my band. Those were crooks. They weren't under bondage like the big companies are now. And the only major company that I went with that was under bonds was when I went to Joe Glazer. See, Glazer wanted me to hold out for big money. And my band could wait for 40, 50 bucks a night. And he didn't want it. He wanted me to stay out for big money. So consequently, I had to come back where I could make a living with the band. And Ella Fitzgerald had Mo Gale to meet me up at the Safari Ballroom. And we all met up there and Mo Gale. In those days I was such a young man, I didn't have anyone to advise me. And I always thought that I had got stung a couple of times when Mo Gale asked me to surrender 35% of my earnings after it got to a certain amount of money. Which, if I had accepted it, I would be making far more money than just saying, well, no, I'm not going to give you 35%. Because it started at 10%, say for $150 a night, and 200 you would get 15% and modulated up to where it got to 35%. But when it got to 35%, it was in the thousands.
Yeah.
And then I could have stayed with Gale's office, but no.
And I told her I appreciated her doing what she did for me, but I didn't think I was ready for that.

Which is another mistake. Another mistake is not taking Ella Fitzgerald in my band when I was playing at the Vendo. In New York? That's in New York? Oh, this was in New York, but not New York City. This was in Buffalo, New York. I was playing at the Vendo and at the Buffalo in Buffalo, New York. But now when Ella had Gale to meet me, this was in New York City at the Savoy Ballroom. See, Ella had already gotten to be a pretty established performer, and by being close friends, she was going to do me a big favor, which it was. And I'm sorry that I didn't accept it in those days. I possibly would have gone a lot further than I did. Well, some of the bookers were national. Well, that's why we were going ahead and we were talking about these bookers. Yeah. What do you start to ask me?
I want to know if some of them were national or some of them just had little territory or something?

No, they just was individuals. We'd book anywhere where they could. When we got to Florida, maybe some guy would know a few of the spots over there. He would book us. In Little Rock, Arkansas, we had a fellow named Brady Bryant that knew most of the places around there. He would book them out. But not any bonded book in the United States. Those things came up way later.
I was wondering if Goldberg had contacts in New Mexico and Arizona.
No, Goldberg confined himself in Texas. His home is now in Dallas where he originally was from. And he confined himself there to the hotels. He was familiar with the managers of the hotels.
What about on the West Coast?

Another big mistake was not going to the West Coast. I was offered a contract at the Culver City. Cotton Club in Culver City. And I didn't want to go West. I thought maybe New York would have a bigger effect on my music career. That's a mistake because from Culver City came bands like Lionel Hampton and Les Hype. Bands like that, you see. Well, I could have gone to California and possibly made greater strides than going to New York. But I don't know. It might have amounted to the same thing. Not having enough intelligence, I'll say, in regards to book us the know-how and know how to deal with these people. I imagine the same thing might have happened there. Double-crossing and stealing.
Oh, yeah.

That's what happened in New York. This double-crossing and this Al Travis stealing everything he could. Booking my band five and six nights. Five and six different towns on the same nights. But he was getting deposits off of all of them. We weren't seeing the deposits. We played one town. A lot of people were looking for us. We didn't show up there when we got a lawsuit through the union.
We once talked about being stranded. If you did lose all your money and all that. There was a German man you would wire for money?

No, I know what you're referring to. This was in Texas. That was in East Bernard. I can't recall his name right now. But not being stranded. He was a friend of mine. He told me whenever you need something, just wire it. But now the time that I actually was stranded was when I was with this Chauncey Holland or Al Travis I think. It was in a little town in Carbondale, Illinois. And there was an old lady there, another lady. She liked me and she liked the band. So we were living with her and we didn't have another engagement anyway. So I took my wife's ring and soaked it for $50, hocked it for $50 and bought an old Pontiac. So I told the fellas, well I'm going to light out and we're going back to Texas. I'm going and book the band. So the little lady said, well okay, I'll take you having three meals a day, man, and sleep. And they all were happy. Nobody cried. I said, well the old man's going and he'll straighten it out. So on the way I break down about 10 miles out of Clarksville, Missouri. And this old Pontiac just went to pieces. Well I didn't know what to do then. Because I had my wife with me and my little son. He was about 9 or 10 years old. So my wife has always been skeptical of her color, even though she shouldn't be. And we knew that the hotels didn't accept Negroes. But however, with my nerve and my craziness, I guess they say, I went to this hotel. And asked the man there, did he have a room that I had a wife in the kitchen? So sure. So he went on up and said he got the room. But she never came out of the room all night. And my poor little boy, whatever they had to do, they did it in the room. So I said, well in the morning I'm getting out here and I'm going to find some Negro residents. So I got out and I started walking and I come downtown and I meet a fella. And I walked up to him and I said, don't get all excited. And I said, I'm not white. I said, I'm a Negro and I'm in trouble. I said, I'm trying to find some place to put my family up. I'm stranded. So he told me about a place across the track, which was the old, we're telling you where to go for the Negroes on the other side of the track. And I walked, I started walking so finally I got over and I looked at this house that I thought it was. And it was Cadillacs in the garage. I said, this can't be the place. So I went next door and this was the place where I was supposed to have gone. This fella says, well no. He says, I can't help you out, but I have a cousin on the other side of town. You go and see her. So I started to walk. Now I'm worrying about this, my boy and my wife in the hotel. So finally I get on the street that he told me and I see this woman on a porch. She was rocking. So I went up there. I bid the time of day and I told her who I was. I gave her my story. Oh, she says, yes, go on back and get your wife and kid by all means and come on. So I came on back and brought them there and was one of the most beautiful relationships that I have ever met on the road. Her mother was a real elderly lady in her late 70s. And she was a young person. Somewhere around my age possibly, maybe a few years younger. And they took us in and I finally got somebody to fix the old automobile. I found a burnt motor that was in perfect condition. And it took me a week to get this done. In the meantime, these people were feeding me and my family. And my son used to go out in the yard. There was a great big apple tree there. And the train would stop. They had got used to seeing him out there waving. And the conductor would stop the train to wave at my son, little boy. And then he would take off again. So finally when everything, I contacted the band and told them what the problem was. I said, sit tight. And I said, I had everything ready in just a little short time. They called me and told me the automobile was ready. And I came and told the people that I had to leave. And boy, they were sorry just like it was a son and a daughter leaving. And they even gave me some money to travel with because I didn't have anything. So over a period of years, we became really close friends. And I would write to them and they would write to me. And finally in the old ladies, old days, real old, she was 90. I took a trip to Chicago to see my uncle Nat and we stopped. They were living in Quincy, Illinois. And old as she was, why, she got up every morning and fixed breakfast and fixed dinner. And she was in her 90s. Finally after we got back to San Antonio, maybe about a year or two later, then she passed. But we're still in touch with the daughter. Those are one of the happy things that you like to talk about. Now even though you're stranded, there's someone there to lift you up, you know. So you're not lost altogether.
And you did make out when you got the money somehow?

Oh yeah, sure. I went right ahead and I booked a band, Rice-Bray, all through Texas. But like I said, I had a lot of nerve. I would go to the Western Union and send a telegram to the promoter. And you would accept it, man.
You know, I found out something this morning. At least I read it in the book. I don't know if it's true or not. It said Aaron Bell's mother was from New Orleans.
Who is Aaron Bell?
He's a bass player with Duke Ellington.
Aaron Bell?
Yeah, there was a lot of Bells. I thought he was an Okie from Muskogee, you know.
Yeah, but I never really would. You don't know any Bells from Muskogee?
No. They had a whole family. She was a music teacher.
No, you got the wrong person. You talking about Pettiford?
Well, he was from there too. Oscar Pettiford? Yeah. I don't know the Bell.
You don't know the Bell family.
I know there are a lot of musical families around there.

Well, Oscar Pettiford, that's the band I was supposed to go with when I went to Troy's band. Oh, you were going with the Pettiford? They wanted me. And I had Richard McCarthy from here and Lucian Johnson. And I told them what I was going to do, so I told Richard, I said, Richard, I can get you in this little band if you want to stay. He wanted to come back to New Orleans. So I talked to Pettiford and he only just wanted me in the band. And I told him, no, I had already told Troy that I was going to join him and I didn't want to go against my word. Which Pettiford was this? This was Oscar's mother, Oscar Pettiford. And his sister was the decisive one. I can't recall all her names right now, but it was a family band. The daddy played the drums, the mother played the piano. And Harry was Harry Pettiford, great tenor player. And then Oscar was the young one, the bass player, he was the young Pettiford.
Did you know the biases? Sure, all of them were there?
No, they're from Birmingham, aren't they? I thought they were from Muscogee too.
I thought they were from Birmingham. They may be, I know. I know that Don was around there or something. Don Bias? Yeah, there's so many Midwestern musicians.
Well, I always connected Don Bias with the brothers, Doug Bascom and his brother. They may have been, I don't know.
Ron Birmingham, I'm sure.
Now you have another one, Christian, the guitarist? Yeah, Charlie. Charlie Christian. Well now he was from Oklahoma City. A lot of people said Tulsa, where are any fields this from?

I had a whole bunch of names of people that I wanted to ask you about, that played around Texas and Kansas City and Connecticut. Did you ever think of the name of T Holder's singer? Do you know who that would have been? Featero?
He was with T Holder. Oh sure, that band there is where Andy Craig slipped away from T Holder. Oh yeah. And that's the same musicians.
Yeah, so he had played T Holder. What about A.G. Gonday's reputation? What kind of drummer was he?
Great drummer, left-handed drummer. It was great in those days.
And who did he play with? Tren? Mostly with Tren. Tren. That was the only band I've known God I'd ever play with.
And you had a Jimmy Westbrook out of, what's the name of that, Waco, Texas. And that's the one where Herschel was with them. He was called the T&T Band.
Yeah, I was going to ask you about that band. You were talking about the Tren. Right.
Well Herschel was playing alto in that band. And Jimmy Westbrook was playing the drums. He was not the left-handed drumming.
Who else was in the T&T? I can't recall. Big band, a small band?
Well in those days, yes. Ten pieces were considered big.
Why did you go on that train? You went to Wichita? No, no.

That was during the days of the, what do you call it, the Dixie Series. We used to have Texas and Louisiana, we played at the winners from each, and we were going to Dallas. That's where you first went? That's where we stopped. Those guys had me playing my horn all night on the train, Herschel and a few of the others. And that's when we got off to Dallas. That's where Herschel separated from me, went on with the T&T band. And I had Lucien and McCarthy, Richard. And we played at one of the roughest joints in Dallas. In the real ghetto. And shoot and everything else. And being a kid, I wasn't used to this, but I guess I just overlooked it. And I must have stayed there about six months before I finally got in connection with Troy Florida. I took Ben O' Kennedy quit his band, I took Ben O' Kennedy's place.
Now what kind of band was that that you were there, with McCarthy and Jeff?

Well they had a piano player there, and Verney Johnson was playing in front of them, boy. And they just added me to what they had there with my little group. That's why the guy picked me up for the game. And they used to add to some of the musicians that had quit him. And the trumpet player that was there before was a fellow named Frenchy. Oh yeah, Paul D. Christian.
Paul D. Christian, right. But that band, what was the name of that band?
It wasn't right in the name.
No leader? I was supposed to be. Just thrown together and you took over.

Just thrown together, right. There was a lot of musicians out there that people have really overlooked, and I consider him one of the greatest alto players I have ever heard. And he was a real, real close copier. Well he wasn't copying because in those days Johnny Hodges was just coming along. And this guy played fantastic just like Johnny Hodges, Fred Murphy. And nothing has ever been said. Well there's so many, Dick, that you could sit out and reminisce over these guys that you know that really could play that have been forgotten. Possibly it's one of these things like we have with Joe Phillips here, a fellow that's reluctant to talk. Maybe he's not a talker. So consequently he goes unnoticed. Yeah.
Well you have to put yourself before the public. Well a lot of them don't.
They don't know how to do it.
Well you can't even get them to audition. Right, right, right. Which reminds me, did you ever make many auditions?

Oh man, that was a common thing, auditions. I tell the band, listen man, we've got an audition tomorrow. Just like the Three Deuces, we went down and played the Three Deuces in Chicago where Tatum was playing and we must have played a half day for the boss man. We auditioned here in New Orleans to play on the boat. And Captain Vern Stryfus came to hear us up at the Pelican. He used to bring the metronome with him to see if your tempos varied. He was tough. Sure they did this on the boat. If any of these guys can remember, they watched the metronome to see if the bands varied.
What boat was this, which one? President. Did you work on the President?
We worked, but only one night. A lot of people connect me with going up and down the river as a sustained thing, but I didn't.
You would never own other riverboats then?

Well, the capital. You owned the capital. Right, but however the boat here was the Sesquahanna. Yeah, I heard. That's on Lake Pontchintrain. That was with Bigfoot, Bill, Phillips, when I was just beginning.
Yeah, you tell me about that and meeting Buddy Petit and all those things.
Right, right, over there at his home.
Yeah, all that, but the riverboats was not a big thing with you and the capital and the- No, no, no. And on Austin.
Not as a sustained thing, maybe a one night deal or something like that. I see.
Back to Texas, were there many bands around Austin?

No, the biggest bands there was Troy, that is the Negro bands you're referring to, right? Either way. Well, I can't vividly remember the big white bands. One of them I remember was Furman Walden, and then it was Troy and it was Trent. Those were the names. Of course, we had the Oleana Orchestra in Galveston. And that's the one that Claude Kennedy went to. Yeah, I don't know the Oleana. No, it didn't last long.
It's a good name.
Yeah, well, Oleana is named after the Galveston. That's the tree there. Oleana tree, so the band picked up the name.
Did you ever hear of the Deluxe Melody Boys?
Melody Boys.
Yeah, Deluxe. Right. Where were they from?
I don't remember.
I don't remember offhand. You look these things up and then you forget where you got your questions from.
Right, right. I don't know where the Deluxe Band was.
Did you know the Corleys, George Corley and Reginald Corley?

Sure, Corley Brothers. Who were they? Musicians. Well, one of these musicians we have here, the Corley Brothers were from Austin. That's their home. And they attended Sam Houston College, which is gone now. It's a combined college now with Deluxe. But that's where these brothers went. Yeah, well, were they, did they have a band there on? Yes, they did around there. Local band. Didn't travel too much. What about Eddie and Sugarloo?
Did you ever hear them?

Oh, I worked with them in the little town of Longview, Texas. How long were they with them? Oh, we played maybe a week or two at a time. And that's when I was with Troy's band. And we made those, after we tried his band I think, I might have made something with Eddie and Sugarloo on one of the recordings, but I can't find it.

I might have it at school. Maybe so I'll be fine if I'd like to hear it. I think they made the KWK blues or something like that. Yeah. But, and I, you know, I can't remember offhand, but I had the old vocalion and then it got broken.
Well, the old vocalions, that was the first one. And then it went into the OKEH, which just said OKRUNS. Well, because that's the one that Troy made the Chattanoid blues on and also Dreamland.
And now we get on to the Happy Black Aces. Do you remember them? Gene Colley's band? Gene Colley. Colley, C-O-Y. Gene Colley. No? No. That may not have ever been a big name.
No, it could have been.
Yeah, well, and what about the Blue Moon Synccapades? Blue Moon Chasers.

Yeah, Chasers. Chasers. That's Bud Johnson and his brother. That was in Dallas. Yeah. A young band. And I used to go up there and they wanted me to come and blow my horn. I'd go and blow my horn and they, after I played in the race, that was Bud Johnson and his brother, Cag. Cag Johnson. And then there was a banjo. One of the guys got killed in the train wreck. One of the banjo. I can't remember all the names right fast. Oh, don't worry.
You know, Clyde Carr was out there in Texas.
Well, Clyde is from Newson. That's the one I was just asking about that's at the college here.
He's from Houston, is he?
Sure. Ask him. I'm almost sure he is. He's a Texas boy.
I, you know, I know him and his son, but I never talked to him.
You had more than one. You had brothers. Clyde Carr brothers. Clyde and his brothers. Oh, yes. And they played around Texas.
I'm almost sure that his home is used to.
How was Buster Smith in those days? Buster's the greatest. He's still the greatest.
He plays now, but he has lost most of his teeth and he's playing on the organ, but he's also

playing. Besides, the other day, Frank Drake's called me and wanted me to come up to New York and do a session and he wanted me to get hold of Buster's number. But I don't know what happened to that thing, Dick. But he wanted to get Buster's number. And I gave him Buster's number. But I don't know what happened to that thing, Dick. I never was called to go to this session. And I was helping him. And I talked to John Hardy. You remember John Hardy? Yeah. And he said, I don't know what happened to that thing. I don't know what happened to that thing. I never was called to go to this session. But he wanted to get Buster Smith and all the old-timers. And I was helping him to talk to John Hardy. Yeah, he was in my band. But he's a teacher and he's reluctant to leave and go anywhere. reluctant to leave and go anywhere. So I don't know, maybe still in Macon, I'm going to talk to Frank when I get back to San Antonio.
What did Buster Smith sound like then? What did he sound like?
You never heard?
Well, I've heard him on records, but you know, I... Gee whiz, he was a tremendous arranger.

But he's one of the first clarinetists that would play like, oh, Buster Biel and Noah and fellas like that. And there was a clarinetist, I'm trying to think of his name, in Dallas. He left and went to Europe.

When you once told me there was a Buster Biel in Texas, it was not the same guy that was with Henderson. No, it was different. That may be the same name. I just wondered if he used strange harmonies or Buster Smith, you know, they compare him with Charlie Parker and all that.

Well, not that type of playing, no, but he was a fantastic musician as far as tonation and knowing his instrument because he could also do good arranging. He was responsible for Con Basie's theme song, One O'Clock Jump. He wrote that and Basie went ahead and like the other people done, just went ahead and said, it's his number, but it's actually Buster Smith song. I didn't know. That's right. Well, I see in those days, Con Basie was around there with the Blue Devils.
