Okay, it's going on the third real of Don Alba. It's August the 6th, 1973. Day after your birthday, huh? Day after your birthday, that's right. Let me see, we were talking back there about Buster Smith and all that. What about Chalk? Did I ever ask you about Chalk? Drinking Chalk? Did you ever hear of that? Chalk houses?

Well, you mean Chalk, you talking about Chalk the beer? Yeah. Oh yeah, I thought you were talking about somebody's name. That's the beer we used to drink, Chalk beer. That's a homemade beer, homebrew. It was in the speakeasers.
And they always call that Chalk? Chalk brew. I never had known them like much. They had speakeasers out in Texas.
Oh yeah, in those days, speakeasers.
Do you have different neighborhoods in San Antonio? Like, was it anything like New Orleans?

Yes, east side, west side, north side. Same thing that you find all over in the United States, the areas. That's what you're referring to, areas. Right. Mm-hmm. In San Antonio, it's the east side. The west side is predominantly Mexicans. The north side is predominantly white. And the south side, sort of a mixed area.
Well, I find things are less mixed now than they were when I came here, like, 24 years ago in New Orleans. Like what? Seems like housing is more segregated now.

It seems to me that it's, that's what it's going back to. I can't answer that. I don't know why. Myself personally, I wish it had never gone back. I wish it had continued to go forward as it had started.
But you do have some mixed neighborhoods.
Well, San Antonio is really, as far as being integrated in areas, it is getting faster that way. But there's still reluctant, like you say, to go into these areas.
Oh, whatever happened to Trent now?
Trent died in his hometown, Fort Smith all this long.
But did he break his band up or were they going to decline or what?
Well, his band broke up in the early 30s. And one of his men just recently died in New York, Crook, the banjo player. And Leo Mosley is still jobbing in New York. He's doing a fantastic job.
What about a band like Trent? I've heard of Trent's number two band somewhere.
Oh, just some guy picked up Trent's name and used it. Trent never had a number two band. Yeah, well... As far as I can remember.

I know, the guys would get together and call themselves the young... Right, right. ...the Cedar Orchestra here, the young... It's just a branch. A branch. It's a branch. Right. And, but that wasn't a common thing there in Jackson.
No, no, it wasn't. Because you only had one Troy Floyd, you only had one Don Albert, and there was no substitutes or things like that.
But when you got extra work, suppose you got two jobs in the same night, would you give to somebody you knew? I don't know.

Unfortunately, that never happened too often. Just one time, I think that I can remember, when Walter Barnes did the job in the place where they were burned. I ran in Natchez. Well, I was supposed to play that job. But instead I was playing in another little town. I can't call the name of the town, it was about a hundred miles from that. So I couldn't get to that job. So maybe, might have been for the better. I remember the place. I remember it vividly. And I was going to that same dance hall, freezing in the morning, and would light that very stove that caught fire. Not knowing and not feeling like that might have happened.
Yeah. Well, you just took that for granted. Right. When I have those old stoves. Right.
And it was cold, so we had to have them. Yeah.
I've been in places in New Orleans like that. Really?
Oh, yeah.
Big old dance hall. Yeah. They got real cold, you'd see the smoke coming out of the horns of the guys. Right, right.

Well, I've seen the times when we had to play where we had to keep all my pieces in our pockets. Right. To keep them warm. Did you have to play any other though that way? Yeah, we played with mosquito balls over our face. We played a dance in Port Arthur, Texas. Had a swarm of mosquitoes came in and we were out on the pier. And we covered our faces with mosquito balls to play. Oh, Dick, it was hell in those days. I wish sometime that I could just sit out and spend maybe about two, three, four days and go over the whole entire area that I covered. And I would like to have men like, say, Cottrell. And Lloyd Glenn incidentally has a book. I told him I wanted to send it to you. It has the amount of money that we made from night to night. You would be surprised. How the hell you lived on this man? And he has it.
Is he living in California?
Yeah, he was with me in San Antonio. We spent a couple of days together.
He's still in the music business in California. I think he's getting bigger.
I think he's getting a recognition of it that he should have gotten years ago.
How many times did your band break up? One time.

Only one time it really broke up. It really broke up. That was here when I just got tired. Being in just Jit by everybody and I pulled a bus up here on Euro Street where my wife was born. And that's where this Chauncey Holland came and asked me to revive my band and he got to binge it for you to finance it. And that was the only time until I actually gave it up in 1940. Maybe it was another mistake. Because two years later, well possibly not two years, there was another boom come up. Con Basis stayed in so for me. He just remained with his big band. And I went into civil service. And that's where I've been sentenced. Are you asking me something about Fats Martin? Or have you ever talked about it?
Yeah, I've asked you about it.
You asked me something in front of Freddie yesterday.
Yeah, but you said Freddie and he played a dunk.
Well, I think that if you ever heard Fats Martin and you would listen to Freddie, you'll find out it's the same identical beats and everything else.
Yeah, well of course I wanted Freddie to tell me about it. Freddie said, oh, see, Don. That's the man you tell me about it.
Well, I consider Freddie one of the finest drummers that I've ever had the opportunity of working with. By the same token, I believe Fats was the greatest.
I think, well I enjoy Freddie and every kind of job I've ever heard of. Oh yeah.
The brass band. Yeah, sure. Freddie is one of the greatest.
All-round drummers. I've never heard of him play in any shows, but I guess he could do that. Well, I imagine.
I've had him play in shows at the Keyhole. Mm-hmm.
Did you, when you came back from time to time, did you have any fans ever in the 40s for, you know, just to say a one night job? Or would you appear as a guest any time?

The only time I became interested in playing my horn again is when Joe Moray is asking me to come and make the Southland record. I had stopped playing all together and just laid the horn down. But when this came about, and no, I'll have to go back a little further. What's his name over at the Preservation Hall that takes the interview? It was my good friend. Bill Rosso. He plays the violin.
Bill Rosso.

Yeah, Bill came to San Antonio and he interviewed me. And he asked me, why don't you play your horn again? And I said, well, I don't see anywhere where I can play what I know how to play. He said, man, it's going to come back. So finally, I said, well, okay, I'll take a shot. I kind of got my horn out and I started to practice. And then Joe Moray, like I said, was responsible for me being as active now as I am, plus a low influence from, what's his name? We just mentioned. Bill Russell. Bill Russell. Okay.
What about people like the Alamo City Jazz Band or the Happy Jazz Band? Anybody out there in Texas, did you play with them ever?

I'm responsible for them organizing that band. Which one? The album? The album. The album. The album. Both of them. Both of them. Both of them. Because they came to me to make an album. And little Jim Cullen wasn't even playing. So I agreed to make the album. But the thing that happened on, as I told you before, I let those men do most of the playing. And when they brought it to Frank Triggs, a friend of mine in Columbia, they said, well, I don't have enough of Don Alvin on. And no voice. And now we're in that solo. So from that then, we had a falling out of personal things. I thought they were real prejudice, which was proven to me on one of my engagements with them on Mike Wallace's program. And so I just pulled away.
And you didn't play with Alamo City? No. No. No.

And I only played maybe once or twice with Jim because, like I said, the reception that I got from them wasn't what I thought it should be. And it caused a close relationship with people. It was one of these distant things. And I just stayed as close as I could. But I have a, I will say this, that Jim Cullen was a nice fella, a likable fella. And to me, he wasn't the greatest clarinetist in the world. But he did have a soulful feeling in his playing. And it was pleasing. He could enjoy it. And I went to his grave site.
What about the Hemisphere?

You played that, didn't you? Yeah, but it was a hard struggle, Dick. Dick, I had to fight all the way up to the Congressman Gonzalez to get a spot in there. I was the only Negro that actually put on his show at the Hemisphere. The only one. Now there were one, there were individuals, single individuals like this, maybe one, two, or three. But for the size of the, of the world's fairs, it was supposed to be with one representation, not all.
And they didn't bring anybody in from out of town on their way?
No, not any Negro. Well, like I said, maybe one at a time. Oh, I see.
Same. What about Peg Keller? Who we were going to talk about?
Oh, Peg was great. He was a fantastic, I mean a great piano player. He was from Houston. But he used to come sit in a band in Chadland in the twenties. But Peg died recently.
But how would you describe him? Would you compare him with...

It's hard to compare an individual that has a style of his own. The same way you'd ask me to compare Lloyd Glenn possibly with Eddie Hewitt, which is two different things all together. Or the same with Peck Kelly. You couldn't say Peck was like so and so. Peck was like Peck Kelly. Was he fast? Yeah, very fast. Then you had Alan Vann that was with Troy's band. You can't compare him with Peck, but he played songs that Peck played too like Kitten on the Keys and things like that which was big in those days.
Did the Desdems ever get down there? Dan Desdems or Clarence Desdems? Did you ever meet them?
Clarence Desdems from here? No. Dan, you never did meet up with them? No.
There was a band called the Southern Serenagers. Did you ever hear of them?

The Southern Melody Boys or the Southern Centipaders? It could have been any name. Both of them. There were two. Southern Melody Boys and the Southern Centipaders. And who were they? Millard McNeil. And he had the Southern Melody Boys. A.J. Johnson went into the Southern Centipaders. And it was the same person. I'll just change the names there.
And where were they from? San Antonio. I see. I think that's the band that made a record with them. They just didn't know anything about them.
Well, maybe they might have had Boots and his Buddies. See, all that's the same thing.
Oh, they're all the same guys. I've got so many questions, I know we're never going to get to them. Did you know Jack T. Gardner in Texas? Oh, yeah, sure. Jack's son is there, yeah.
Oh, yeah? Where is he? He, he, last time I talked with Jack Jr., he was operating a motel. He plays a beautiful drum roll.
And Terry Shand, did you ever know? Oh, yeah, that's one of the old bands.
Yeah, right. Herman Wallman, Terry Shand, and you had some other bands, I can't call their names right now. Rex Priest.
Who was Jack with? Was he with his own band when you first met him? Or was he with the...

Jack T. Gordon? Yeah, when you first met him. No, I don't remember when I first met him, but I remember him when he was playing with Glenn Gray's Castle. I was up in Indianapolis. Ziggy Ellman and that group. And they would come over to where I was playing at the sunset. They were playing at the theater at Alta. And that's why I told you about T. Gordon and I playing out in the snow together. I don't think you ever told me. I didn't. Well, they came down there and they came into the sunset and we rushed up there and said, Man, go ahead and get your horn. I've never seen this before in the south. He said, it's snowing out there. Ziggy got his horn and Jack got his horn and got mine. I forgot who the other fellow was. There was four damn fools out there playing in the snow. Just for fun. Just for the fun. I let the snow fall on you, man.
When you were on the road like that, did you ever meet Benny Goodman or Tommy Dorsey or Don Stratton?

No, we met Bob Cosby and what was his bad cats? I don't know if you ever would remember that, but we were doing fairly good and we had enough to eat. Bob Cosby didn't and we just stopped on the road and shared what we had. They were hitting it pretty hard.
Yeah, well you knew some of those guys probably by sight as kids. Right, right. Because a lot of those fellows were from New Orleans. Yeah, yeah. What about Don Redman? You never met him?
I played with Don. Well, not played with him. He worked along with me in Detroit, Michigan. That's where you had your big bands like Bikini Cotton Pickers, Fletcher, Harrison.
Oh, you'd be alternating at the...
Different clubs. Different clubs.
What about a sweet band like Alambardo?
Never met him. I've never met him in my life.
What do you mean by an automatic player? You've told me about guys that were just automatic players.

I mean this, that he's just... Well, for instance, what's his name? Tim. Tim says he can play, but he has to have music before him. That's an automatic player. He has to have it. I was the same way. Like I told you, you have to sit down and by yourself some time. And play the number that you read at first. And then try throwing it aside and try and play. Make your own improvisions.
So, little songs, turns, and twists. Yeah. Make you, you know, they'll say better they hear. That's sort of so.
So, get your own individual style. Something personal.
When you come back, you visit your family's graves and the shrines and things in our town?

Yes, I do. You see, I have had so many blessings in my life that I made a promise years ago. And this was through my mother and my sister. I don't know what's happened over the last few years. Every time I'd come here, why, she was ready to go with me. Now she doesn't go. But it's one of the promises that I made. I know she'll listen to what I'm saying. That whenever I come here, I would visit the graves of my relatives and pay them the respect that I owe them. Then visit the shrine that my mother introduced me to. And the shrine, actually, which is my patron saint, St. Jude. Those are the first stops on my agenda. And the next stop is to try to get the test with Dick Allen, which has become a problem.
You can't reach me through too much. Well, your patron saint is a... St. Jude. Patron saint in lost colleges. Right.
Impossible cases. Impossible cases. You might ask my sister why she doesn't go with me anymore. She might have an answer to it. Why you don't visit anymore, is that true? Huh?
I was always pushing this concert.
Because I was selling the tickets. She sold most of the tickets, man. She wanted to know if I was coming.

I couldn't miss it. I don't think I've ever missed one of your concerts. Oh, gosh. Well, some of these fellas that played with him, I know almost nothing about. We talked about Billy Douglas and Alvin Alcorn. Howell Harding, you said, was from out of Texas.
He's out of Dallas. Out of Dallas. Whatever happened? Still there. He's still there? He's not in the music community.
Did he play with any other bands?

Yes, I got it. When he came to Dallas, the day that we first arrived in Dallas, and he asked for a job here, he had just left a band out of Oklahoma City, but I don't remember what was the name of the band. Might have been Alvin Walls. See, he died. That was another one of the West Texas, I mean, Western bands. Midwest bands. Alvin Walls. Oh, yeah. He's a great, great alto player and a great writer.
I've heard about him.
Oh, he was great, but he died. He died recently in Detroit. Which other one?
Well, what about the trombone play?
Which one?
Well, all of them.
Well, you had Frank Jackay. Strictly a section man. Yeah. Geechee Robinson. Where did Frank Jackay come from? Lake Charles, Louisiana. Cousin to Illinois.
Who did he play with, Frank?
Mostly with me. Mostly with you.
And Geechee Robinson, you once told me about, you were with Fletcher Henderson for a while.
After he left my band. Yeah.
Who else was he with?
Oh, so many bands. You can't have to have a typewriter or something, an ad machine for the bands Geechee played, but you couldn't stay.
He jumped from band to band?
Yeah, peculiar, what you're going to say, he's always getting arguments of, things with band. I believe he stayed with me longer than anyone he stayed with.
And Nick Turner, who did he play with?
Well, Nick was around here. Nick never played too much with anyone.
Well, he went on up north then.
He went with me as a bass player.
Yeah, but then afterwards he went up north or something.
But he didn't play with anyone. No, he died like I told you in this little, that stick in this little town.
Oh, he actually died.
No, he didn't die there, he died in Chicago.
Oh, I see. Well, there's another bass player named Turner. Not in my band. I must have been more confused, you know. Because... Could be two guys with the same name.
Yeah, well, we call him Nick. What was Nick's name? Henry Turner.

Henry Turner was his name. Yeah. Henry Johnson, Henry Turner. Yeah. And, alright, let's look at the reeds now. What about your altos? Which ones? The first was Arthur Dermy. Well, alright, your first was Arthur Dermy. Oh, the first was Arthur Dermy. Yeah, I know about him playing around here.
Yeah, well, Arthur played all over Lonnie with Arthur taken sick and had to leave.
And he... When I knew him, I just knew him and it wasn't far from here. I guess he had a restaurant on St. Bernard.
Not a restaurant, he lived by a restaurant. Oh, then stuff. Yeah, he lived... Well, then stuff.
Right. But he was right along when I used to see him.
And then there was Phil Tiller, Herbert Hall, and Cottrell.
Yeah. And what happened to Phil Tiller?
Phil Tiller died recently in New York. Did he continue... He's from Little Rock, Arkansas. No, he stopped. He got out altogether. When he stopped, he stopped playing.
Who was he with before he got here?
He played with all the bands in Arkansas.
Was he ever with Trent? No.
Arkansas.
Dink Taylor? Dink was from Little Rock.
And who did he play with? Most of those bands in Arkansas, but I can't remember. Yeah, yeah.
And did he continue on after he left you?

Yes, he did, but I don't know what ever happened to him. Nobody else knows. You ask everybody what happened to Dink, and nobody can tell you. Dink wasn't his name. That was a nickname. And I asked for his name, and I couldn't tell you to save my life.
I think I found it somewhere. I know Herbert Hall has gone on with Eddie Condon.

Yeah, he's getting ready to settle in Texas. He's going to come south again? That's right. They bought his wife. We introduced his wife to him when we first came to San Antonio, Texas. And he married her right around 20, around 29 or 30. And her parents are from a little town of Bernie, and they had a lot of land up there. And they willed it to his wife. Mm-hmm. So Herbert visited me sometime this year. Mm-hmm. And they built a fabulous home up there, and he's leaving New York altogether. Well, I can understand that.
He wants to settle.
Yeah. Yeah. Jimmy Condon just died, and that's the guy that he played with most of the year. Mm-hmm.
Sure, he had his rough moments up there. Yes, he did.

New York was not easy. But fortunately he fell into his brother's footsteps. See, Edmund's name was big. Mm-hmm. So there wasn't any problem, because Herbert can play. Oh, I agree with you that. So there wasn't any problem for him to pick up in his brother's footsteps.
I'm trying to think of who I've ever heard of him playing with in the way of big bands other than yours.
Oh? Yeah. Who have you?
Yeah. None. He played around... He's confined to small bands. He played around in Baton Rouge some, I think he told me. Of course, was there, or whatever.

Oh, well, that's where he's from. Yeah. But not after he left my band. Yeah, I guess so. He's going back to before he came to my band and Reserva and up in there. There was nine brothers, all of them were musicians. Yeah. Including the daddy.
Now, Cartrell, we know pretty well, we've got his life story now. So that's the reeds and the brass, the rhythm, Lloyd Glenn.
Well, there's some, a lot of them that you left out that came in later days. Yeah. But you're going to be the original, right?
Yeah, yeah, the main one. Right. I don't know. You had the Pattinson Brothers. Yeah.

From here. No, from Beaumont. Oh, yes. But you had Pattinson here that stayed in the start of John Pattinson. John Pattinson from here. He stayed in the short while. You know John Porter used to play the bass. Really?
He was with you from all of it. He didn't stay.
He didn't want to stay. He didn't want to leave New Orleans. It's funny, he was on the road so much, we showed. Right.
That's what he just got tired of traveling. Right. He didn't want to go anymore. We had enough of that. And Fats Martin tried to hold the band together for a while.
He did. He held the remnants.
Did he continue playing after that? Right. Played until he died.

Well he had his own little group and his wife was the pianist in the band. Never had any great musicians. It was him and her. That was the biggest part of the band. And then they would just pick up any musicians. Fats and Lady Yes got to be a real contrary fellow. Couldn't anybody get along with him. I imagine that's because he was getting sick. And a man gets in a place where he's sick all the time. He becomes irritable and can't get along with anyone. He had this disease, the Bryce disease. But I stayed with him until he died. Got him baptized in the Catholic Church. I was his Godfather. And stayed and I went and carried his body.

He'd go there every night when Juanita would go off to play at this club. He'd go there and sit on the outside to keep Fats company. And Fats was on the last thing. Because he needed to see him alone.

Oh yeah. Well she would tell me to watch Fats. You know, I'd call her and she says, Come on over, I'm going to work. So I'd get over there and all the doors are locked. And so I'd go to the window and I'd eat that. I could raise his head up and tell him my cousin. I said, I don't worry about nothing. I said, if you get to the place where you really need me, I'm breaking the window. I said, well I need him locked all the house. When I'd come back she'd be all surprised. Thought she had left everything and all that. Unfortunately he didn't die while she was calling him to work. And when he did die, I was sitting in the kitchen talking. Jay Golson was one of my arrangers.
He never got the plan that the rest of his family did, huh?
Who?
Jay Golson.
Jay Golson didn't have anybody in the family. Wasn't he related to Benny the Tenno player?
How do you spell his name?
G-H-O-L-S-O-N. He's the only one in the family.
Oh, well I must have the family.
He's still a great arranger. He's still a great arranger. He arranges from Motown. He was a piano player that really wrote the part of my book. It was great, great arrangements. Mm-hmm.
Was he came in after Lloyd then?
Right. No, I, yes he did, after Lloyd. See, Lloyd didn't stay a long, long time. Jay Golson came in. And then from here when I reorganized the band was Lionel Reason. Mm-hmm. That was the pianist.
Did I ever get your father's name? Ferdinand.
Ferdinand, I thought I had. But it's spelled F-U-R-N-E-N-D, Fernand. He wanted to make the distinction between the Ferdinand and Fernand.
I think we just about got the rhythm there except, well, Ferdinand and Dajon.
Well, Dajon, you missed him.
Yeah, no. Did he continue playing?
No, you know, Dajon went into the insane asylum. Yeah. And that's why he died.
Yeah. But that was from your band.
Oh, he started here with my big band. And he left, I sent him home. Must have been tracking. Yes, it was.
It was such a good rhythm section.
It was great. That's what made the band so great. It had a set, a tempo that nobody there ever heard. The tempo was the thing that got my band over.
What kind of a tempo do you use?
Well, we call it America's greatest swing metal.
D&D This is a fourth real hard job. Yeah. August 1972. 73.
Did not ever tell you how his father chastised him, Dick?
The machine's on. The machine's on. Tell us the truth, man.
Did not ever tell you how his father chastised him?
Like what?
When you did something Papa didn't like.
Oh, yeah.
What he made you do. I've got the gun downstairs if you want to go get that.
He had that shotgun walking around the block in my underwear.
That was his punishment.
That was my punishment. That would break my heart.
What would he do?

Hold the shotgun on there and make me walk around the block in my underwear. A little kid, man. I'd be maybe about six, seven, eight, nine years old. And I was so always proud of myself. And that walking around the block in my underclothes was the worst thing that could ever happen to me. Did the neighbors say anything? I guess the neighbors looked at him and laughed, I imagine. But I was too busy crying and noticing anybody looking at me.
Dutch, what did you do? Well, she was too young.
I'm eight years younger than Donnelly.
You don't remember that. No, I was about eight, nine years old.
Yeah, eight or nine years old when this was happening.
You were talking about your band being... Oh, the swing area?

About the swing area. Right. That reminds me of one time when we were going through Florida and the bus had broken down in Mobile, Alabama. I stayed up all night to get it fixed. And consequently, I was tired. So, Dick Taylor started to drive. We were going down to... I think it was mine. We were going through Tallahassee. We had to stop in Tallahassee and get a permit to travel a state. We'd pay a penny a mile to travel a state of Florida. So, when we crossed the bridge, we had a place in the back where the drivers would rest. Whoever drove before resting would get another driver. So, Dick was driving. He was going kind of fast. We hear this siren blowing. So, Dick says, wake the old man up with his white face and bring him up here. The policemen are coming. So, he pulled on the side of the road and I rushed from the back on up to the front and put my cap on. And, Dick got out of the driver's seat and went to the back. So, this policeman drives up on his motorcycle. He looks in there all surprised. He said, are you driving this bus? I said, sure. Well, now, I know that he must have meant that he saw a black face then. You know. But, he was so surprised. He went on. So, he said, what you got in there? A nigger man? I said, no, I got some musicians. I got them under contract. We were going to play a little town in Florida, Miami. And, he said, can they play guitars? I had America's Greatest Swing Band written on the bus. He must have interpreted it as a string band. So, I told him, no. I told him, no. I said, these fellows are under contract. They can't do that. So, he walked around to the bus. I asked for my fire extinguisher. I sent different little stupid questions. And, I answered them. So, he said, well, I didn't think that you were driving this bus. I said, well, who else could drive it? Well, that's another time where I used my complexion to an advantage. I'll say, well, he says, you better hurry up and get this band on through there. He said, when you go to Tallahassee, don't stop. He said, they're looking for a couple of niggers down there that shot a policeman, kill a policeman. And, they might take any one of these out of his bus if it kind of looks like who it was. I guess you know we didn't go through Tallahassee. No, we bypassed Tallahassee. We got down to the next town and we bought the permit, which was permissible, to buy it in the first place where you could stop and tell whoever's in charge of the courthouse how many miles. you're under an assumption that you're going to make a thousand miles. You pay the assumption fee, which is a penny a mile, which wasn't much.
Well, you guys' song were pretty dark in the band.

Oh, yeah, really. Well, Nick was what you call real black Nick was. But, like I say, you know, color doesn't play too much of a part in the world. I thought it shouldn't because I had some brilliant, brilliant men in that band. It was a complacent, Ross Dawg.
Yeah.
And, by the same token, I met some my color that I couldn't even reach in no kind of way.
What about, we were talking about the string bass, too. You say you had the string bass in Texas. Did they have many string bass players?

Mine was, well, you had this fella that was originally from Louisiana. They called him Manoon. I was living in Houston outside, but he wasn't playing too much. But, I brought Jimmy. He left here with me. And, that was the first time they had ever seen a string bass in a band. It was a novelty to them.
They were looking used to tubas out there.
Right, right. Tubas. Well, you'd see Brent Sparks with, with, with, with, with, with Trank. They had a tuba. Most any band had tubas.
Charlie Dixon was playing too. Charlie Dixon was playing too.
Charlie Dixon was playing tuba and playing trombone.
But, never string bass.
Never string bass.
Yeah, I can't think. I don't know. Maybe, had Kelly had a string bass or something?
Not that I can recall.
If it probably was somebody from New Orleans, if he did.
If he did. Yes, it was, but I don't remember having, having a string bass. He did most, he did most of his singles. He was, most of his work was singles.
Well, anybody, in New Orleans, how many string bass players were there in September of 29? When you left?
Quite a number.
It was common here. Common.

Common things. I see. It just was fortunate that I, I, I was able to get to you now. I don't know how I ever got you now. I remember driving up to his house on Annunciation Street. That's how it was. Someone had recommended him. And he just said, yeah, okay. He picked on up and left.
You don't remember where he lived.
We're up on Annunciation Street.
Way up.
Way uptown.
What about who. Who.
